Denver is the principal city of the Denver–Aurora–Lakewood metropolitan statistical area.
The Denver–Aurora–Lakewood, CO Metropolitan Statistical Area had a population of 2,963,821 at the 2020 United States census.
The Denver–Aurora, CO Combined Statistical Area had a population of 3,623,560 at the 2020 U.S. census.
Denver is in the western United States.
Denver is located in the South Platte River Valley on the western edge of the High Plains.
Denver's downtown district is east of the confluence of Cherry Creek and the South Platte River.
Denver is about 12 miles (19 kilometers) east of the foothills of the Rocky Mountains.
Denver is named after James W. Denver, a governor of the Kansas Territory.
Denver is nicknamed the "Mile High City".
Denver's official elevation is exactly one mile (5280 feet or 1609.344 meters) above sea level.
The 105th meridian west of Greenwich passes directly through Denver Union Station.
James W. Denver visited his namesake city in 1875 and 1882.
The greater Denver area was inhabited by several Indigenous peoples such as Apaches, Utes, Cheyennes, Comanches, and Arapahoes.
The United States unilaterally defined and recognized Cheyenne and Arapaho territory from the North Platte River to the Arkansas River in 1851.
The discovery of gold in the Rocky Mountains in Colorado in November 1858 led to a gold rush.
Colorado territorial officials pressured federal authorities to redefine and reduce Indian treaty lands.
A group of gold prospectors established Montana City as a mining town on the South Platte River in what was then western Kansas Territory in 1858.
Montana City later faded quickly, and Auraria and St. Charles City became more prominent.
General William Larimer and Captain Jonathan Cox staked a claim on the bluff overlooking the confluence of the South Platte River and Cherry Creek in 1858.
Larimer named the townsite Denver City to curry favor with Kansas Territorial Governor James W. Denver.
Denver City was intended to be selected as the county seat of Arapahoe County, but Governor Denver had already resigned from office.
The site of these first towns is now occupied by Confluence Park near downtown Denver.
Edward W. Wynkoop came to Colorado in 1859 and became one of the city's founders.
Denver City served as the Arapahoe County Seat from 1861 until consolidation in 1902.
Denver City became the acting territorial capital in 1867 and was chosen as the permanent state capital in a statewide ballot in 1881.
Denver shortened its name to Denver after gaining importance.
Denver was admitted to the Union on August 1, 1876.
The Colorado War of 1864 and 1865 resulted from disagreements over the validity of the Treaty of Fort Wise.
The Sand Creek massacre occurred during the Colorado War against Cheyenne and Arapaho peoples.
The reservation in Eastern Colorado was dissolved after the Medicine Lodge Treaty.
Denver residents could look with pride at their success establishing a supply and service center by the close of the 1860s.
Denver's decision to route the nation's first transcontinental railroad through Cheyenne City threatened its prosperity.
Citizens mobilized to build a railroad connecting Denver to the transcontinental railroad.
Territorial Governor John Evans, David Moffat, and Walter Cheesman spearheaded fundraising for the railroad.
$300,000 was raised within three days of fundraising efforts.
Denver's link to the transcontinental railroad ushered in a new age of prosperity.
Denver prospered as a service and supply center after being linked to the rest of the nation by rail.
The young city grew during these years, attracting millionaires with their mansions.
Denver citizens were proud when the rich chose Denver.
Horace Tabor built the Tabor Grand Opera House in Denver.
Luxurious hotels like the Brown Palace Hotel soon followed.
The influx of new residents strained available housing.
The Silver Crash of 1893 unsettled political, social, and economic balances.
Competition among different ethnic groups was often expressed as bigotry.
Social tensions gave rise to the Red Scare.
Americans were suspicious of immigrants who sometimes allied with socialist and labor union causes.
After World War I, a revival of the Ku Klux Klan attracted white, native-born Americans anxious about societal changes.
Corruption and crime also developed in Denver.
Between 1880 and 1930, Denver's floriculture industry thrived.
This period became known locally as the Carnation Gold Rush.
A state constitutional amendment to allow home rule for Denver was introduced in the legislature in 1901 and passed.
The measure called for a statewide referendum, which voters approved in 1902.
On December 1, 1902, Governor James Orman proclaimed the amendment part of the state's fundamental law.
The City and County of Denver came into being on that date and was separated from Arapahoe and Adams counties.
Rocky Flats Plant produced fissile plutonium "pits" for nuclear warheads between 1953 and 1989.
A major fire at the facility in 1957, as well as leakage from stored nuclear waste between 1958 and 1968, contaminated some parts of Denver with plutonium-239.
A 1981 study by Carl Johnson linked contamination to an increase in birth defects and cancer incidence in central Denver and nearer Rocky Flats.
Later studies confirmed many of his findings.
Plutonium contamination was still present outside the former plant site as of August 2010.
It presents risks to building the envisioned Jefferson Parkway, which would complete Denver's automotive beltway.
Downtown Denver cityscape includes landmarks like Trinity United Methodist Church and the Mile High Center complex.
The Brown Palace Hotel is a historic hotel in downtown Denver.
The Cosmopolitan Hotel was demolished.
Denver was selected to host the 1976 Winter Olympics but voters struck down ballot initiatives allocating public funds, moving the games to Innsbruck, Austria.
In 2010, Denver adopted a comprehensive update of its zoning code.
Denver has hosted the Democratic National Convention twice, in 1908 and 2008.
Denver promoted itself on the national, political, and socioeconomic stage during these conventions.
On August 10–15, 1993, Denver hosted the Catholic Church's 6th World Youth Day, which was attended by an estimated 500,000 people.
Denver is known as the "Queen City of the Plains" and the "Queen City of the West."
Denver's central location between the Rocky Mountains to the west and the High Plains to the east defines its geography.
The city center consists of plains with hilly areas to the north, west, and south.
At the 2020 United States census, Denver had an area of 99,025 acres (400.739 km²), including 1,057 acres (4.276 km²) of water.
Denver is surrounded by Adams County to the north and east, Arapahoe County to the south and east, and Jefferson County to the west.
Denver's nickname is the "Mile-High City."
Its official elevation is one mile (5,280 ft; 1,609 m) above sea level.
The elevation of the entire city ranges from 5,130 to 5,690 feet (1,560 to 1,730 m).
Denver lies 750 miles (1,200 km) from the nearest point of the Gulf of California.
Denver has 78 official neighborhoods used for planning and administration.
The city center is denser, older, and contains more brick buildings.
Neighborhoods farther from the city center were developed after World War II with modern materials and style.
Some recently redeveloped areas have suburban characteristics or are new urbanist developments recreating older neighborhood feel.
Colloquial names like Northside and Westside are not well-known.
The Golden Triangle neighborhood was built on the site of Stapleton International Airport, named after former Denver mayor Benjamin F. Stapleton.
In 2020, the neighborhood's community association voted to change the name from Stapleton to Central Park.
Denver has a continental semi-arid climate with generally low humidity and around 3,100 hours of sunshine per year.
Humid microclimates can be found nearby depending on exact location.
Denver has four distinct seasons with most precipitation occurring from April through August.
The region is subject to sudden weather changes due to its inland location on the High Plains.
July is the warmest month with an average high temperature of 89.9°F (32.2°C).
Summers range from warm to hot, occasionally severe afternoon thunderstorms, and 90°F (32°C) on 38 days annually.
December has an average daily high temperature of 44°F (6.7°C).
Winters consist of alternating periods of snow and very low temperatures with milder weather due to the warming effect of Chinook winds.
Daytime highs occasionally exceed 60°F (16°C) in winter but often fail to reach 32°F (0°C) during cold weather.
Occasionally, daytime highs can even fail to rise above 0°F (-18°C) due to arctic air masses.
On the coldest nights of the year, lows can fall to -10°F (-23°C) or below.
Denver has a high elevation and aridity leading to large diurnal temperature variation throughout the year.
Tornadoes are rare west of the I-25 corridor but occur in suburbs east of Denver and its northeastern extension (Denver International Airport).
One notable exception was an F3 tornado that struck 4.4 miles south of downtown on June 15, 1988.
Denver is home to a wide array of museums including the Denver Art Museum by architect Daniel Libeskind.
The Denver Center for Performing Arts hosts various cultural events.
Denver has numerous art districts like Denver's Art District on Santa Fe and River North Art District (RiNo).
Denver has an active music scene with artists in pop, jazz, jam, folk, metal, and classical genres.
Notable folk artists such as Bob Dylan, Judy Collins, and John Denver lived and performed in Denver during the 1960s and 1970s.
Three members of Earth, Wind & Fire are also from Denver.

Recent Denver-based artists include India Aire, Nathaniel Rateliff & the Night Sweats, The Lumineers, Air Dubai, The Fray, Flobots, Cephalic Carnage, Axe Murder Boyz, Deuce Mob, Havok, Bloodstrike, Primitive Man, and Five Iron Frenzy.
Denver is home to the Denver Record Collectors Expo, a biannual music collectors event.
Denver has gained a reputation as an active, outdoor-oriented city with many residents spending weekends in the mountains for skiing in winter and hiking, climbing, kayaking, and camping in summer.
Denver hosts the annual National Western Stock Show every January at the National Western Complex northeast of downtown.
Denver is known for its dedication to New Mexican cuisine and the Chile.
It is famous for green and red chile sauce, Colorado burrito, Southwest (Denver) omelette, breakfast burrito, empanadas, chiles rellenos, and tamales.
Denver is also known for other types of food such as Rocky Mountain oysters, rainbow trout, and the Denver sandwich.
The Dragon Boat Festival in July, Moon Festival in September, and Chinese New Year are annual events in Denver for the Chinese and Asian-American communities.
Chinese hot pot (huo guo) and Korean BBQ restaurants have been growing in popularity.
Denver has a large population of Mexican Americans hosting four major celebrations: Cinco de Mayo, El Grito de la Independencia, Lowrider show, and Dia De Los Muertos art shows/events.
Denver is known for its tolerance of the LGBTQ community with many gay bars on Colfax Avenue and South Broadway.
Every June, Denver hosts the annual Denver PrideFest in Civic Center Park, the largest LGBTQ Pride festival in the Rocky Mountain region.
Denver has been a setting for TV shows like The Bill Engvall Show, Tim Allen's Last Man Standing, and The Real World.
It was also the setting for the prime-time drama Dynasty from 1981 to 1989.

Denver is home to professional sports teams including the Denver Broncos of the National Football League, Colorado Rockies of Major League Baseball, Colorado Avalanche of the National Hockey League, Denver Nuggets of the National Basketball Association, and Colorado Rapids of Major League Soccer.
The Denver Broncos have sold out every home game since 1970 except for strike-replacement games.
The Colorado Rockies advanced to the playoffs in 2007 but were swept by the Boston Red Sox.
The Colorado Avalanche won three Stanley Cups in 1996, 2001, and 2022.
The Denver Nuggets won their first NBA championship in 2023.
Denver has several additional professional teams including Major League Lacrosse's Denver Outlaws and National Lacrosse League's Colorado Mammoth.
In 2018, the Denver Bandits were established as the first professional football team for women in Colorado.
Denver submitted a bid to host the 1976 Winter Olympics but withdrew, being the first city to back out after winning its bid.
Denver has over 200 parks including City Park and Red Rocks Park known for its scenery and musical history.
Denver has 29 recreation centers providing places and programming for residents' recreation and relaxation.
The Denver City Council is responsible for passing and changing all laws, resolutions, and ordinances.
The mayor can approve or veto any ordinances approved by the council.
The city auditor checks all expenditures and may refuse specific ones.
The Denver Department of Safety oversees three branches: the Denver Police Department, Denver Fire Department, and Denver Sheriff Department.
Denver has a strong mayor/weak city council government structure.
Denver is a consolidated city-county with a nonpartisan mayor elected on a nonpartisan ballot.
Democrats have long dominated the city's politics; most citywide officials are known to be registered with the Democratic Party.
The mayor's office has been occupied by a Democrat since 1963.
All seats in the state legislature are held by Democrats.
Denver is a Democratic stronghold at the federal level, supporting a Democrat for president in every election since 1960 except 1972 and 1980.
Benjamin F. Stapleton was mayor of Denver from 1923 to 1931 and again from 1935 to 1947.
Stapleton International Airport, renamed in his honor, has been replaced by a neighborhood initially named Stapleton.
In recent years, Denver has taken a stance on helping people who are or become homeless under mayors John Hickenlooper and Wellington Webb.
Denver became the first major U.S. city to vote for legalizing private possession of less than an ounce of marijuana for adults 21 and older in 2005.
Denver decriminalized psilocybin mushrooms in May 2019 after a ballot initiative passed with 50.6% of the vote.
Denver hosted the first of three 2012 presidential debates at the University of Denver on October 3, 2012.
Denver will not assist U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents with immigration raids as stated by Mayor Hancock in July 2019.
The City and County of Denver levies an occupational privilege tax (OPT or head tax) on employers and employees.
Denver Public Schools educates approximately 92,000 students in 92 elementary schools, 44 K-8 schools, 34 middle schools, 18 high schools, and 19 charter schools.
The first school of what is now Denver Public Schools was a log cabin that opened in 1859 and later became East High School.

Denver has many colleges and universities including the University of Colorado Denver, Metropolitan State University of Denver, Community College of Denver, Regis University, Johnson & Wales University, and others.
The Denver metropolitan area is served by various media outlets including television stations, radio stations, print newspapers, and online platforms.
Denver International Airport (DIA) serves as the primary airport for the Front Range Urban Corridor surrounding Denver.
DIA opened in 1995 and covers more than 52.4 square miles, making it the largest airport by land area in the United States.
Denver has three general aviation airports: Rocky Mountain Metropolitan Airport, Centennial Airport, and Colorado Air and Space Port.
Denver's relationship with Brest, France, began in 1948, making it the second-oldest sister city in the United States.
